summary: Extends the mapping of PPP onto SONET/SDH to cover virtual concatenation and both high-order and low-order payloads, allowing more flexible bandwidth. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: Fiber links come in fixed sizes. This lets you glue several small ones together and treat them as one bigger pipe for carrying data.

questions: why use virtual concatenation with ppp
subtitle: Lets PPP ride on bundles of small SONET/SDH channels, so a link can be sized to fit the traffic.

tldr.problem: PPP over SONET/SDH could only use a few large, contiguously concatenated signals, so the link was often much bigger or smaller than the traffic needed.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC extends RFC 2615 to allow virtual concatenation, which groups several SONET/SDH channels into one logical link, and to allow both high order and low order payloads. It adds two small physical layer rules: matching path signal labels and a populated multi-frame indicator.
tldr.outcome: PPP links can be sized in steps instead of jumping between a few fixed rates. It builds on RFC 2615 and adds no new security features.

today: RFC 3255 is a Standards Track document published in April 2002, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends the PPP over SONET/SDH mapping of RFC 2615.

sections.title: The Problem with Fixed Link Sizes
sections.content:
RFC 3255 extends the mapping of the Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) onto SONET/SDH, which RFC 2615 defines. Implementations of that mapping had to choose from a short list of contiguously concatenated signals: STS-3c-SPE, STS-12c-SPE, STS-48c-SPE and STS-192c-SPE in SONET, or VC-4, VC-4-4c, VC-4-16c and VC-4-64c in SDH.

The RFC also notes that VC-4-4c and above are not widely supported in SDH networks at present. Virtual concatenation addresses this: it means the right size of SONET/SDH bandwidth can be selected for a PPP link.
sections.plainLanguage: Before this, you could only pick from a few big, fixed link sizes. Virtual concatenation lets you build a link that fits better.

sections.title: SONET and SDH Terms
sections.content:
SONET (North American) and SDH (international) describe much the same structures with different names. The RFC gives an extended version of the equivalence table from RFC 2615.

  • A SONET SPE corresponds to an SDH VC.
  • A SONET VT (1.5, 2 or 6) corresponds to a low order VC (VC-11, VC-12 or VC-2).
  • An STS-1 SPE corresponds to VC-3, and an STS-3c SPE corresponds to VC-4.
  • A trailing nv, as in STS-1-nv or VC-4-nv, marks virtual concatenation of n members.

For more detail it points to Bellcore GR-253-CORE, ANSI T1.105, ANSI T1.105.02 and ITU-T G.707.
sections.plainLanguage: Two groups of engineers gave the same parts different names. The table is a translation list so you can tell which name matches which.

sections.title: Rate Comparisons
sections.content:
Without virtual concatenation, supported PPP links are STS-3c / STM-1 (150Mbit/s), STS-12c (620Mbit/s), STS-48c (2.4Gbit/s) and STS-192c (9.6Gbit/s). The RFC notes that AU-4-4c and AU-4-16c are not generally available in SDH networks at present.

With virtual concatenation, with n from 1 to 64, many more sizes appear. In SONET these are VT-1.5-nv (1.6Mbit/s to 102Mbit/s), STS-1-nv (49Mbit/s to 3.1Gbit/s) and STS-3c-nv (150Mbit/s to 10Gbit/s). In SDH they are VC-12-nv (2.2Mbit/s to 139Mbit/s), VC-3-nv and VC-4-nv with the same ranges as their SONET equivalents.

The RFC then compares how well common service rates fit. For a 100Mbit/s service, a plain STS-3c is 67% efficient, while STS-1-2v is 100%. For a 1Gbit/s service, STS-48c is 42% efficient, while STS-3c-7v is 95%. The SDH table gives the same percentages for VC-4 and VC-3-2v, and for VC-4-16c and VC-4-7v. Higher levels of virtual concatenation are possible, but not necessarily useful.
sections.plainLanguage: If you need a bit more than one bucket holds, you used to have to buy a much bigger bucket and waste most of it. Now you can use two or three small buckets that fit almost exactly.

sections.title: Physical Layer Requirements
sections.content:
Using virtually concatenated SPEs or VCs changes the physical layer rules of RFC 2615 in two minor ways.

First, the path signal label (the C2 byte) for STS-1/VC-3 and above is required to be the same for all constituent channels. With contiguous concatenation there is a single C2 byte. The values should follow RFC 2615. For SONET VT-1.5/2/6 and SDH VC-11/12/2, the path signal label (V5 byte bits 5-7) must likewise be the same for all constituent channels.

Second, the multi-frame indicator (H4) byte is unused with contiguous concatenation for STS-1/VC-3 and above. With virtual concatenation it must be populated as ITU-T G.707 or T1.105.02 describe. For the lower order channels, bit 2 of the path overhead K4 byte is set to the value those standards indicate.
sections.plainLanguage: When you tie pipes together, every pipe must carry the same label, and each one needs a number tag so the pieces are put back together in the right order.

sections.title: Standards Status
sections.content:
ITU-T (SG13/SG15), ANSI T1X1 and ETSI TM1/WP3 developed a global standard for SONET/SDH high order and low order payload virtual concatenation. It is defined in ITU-T G.803, G.707 and G.783, ANSI T1.105 and T1.105.02, and ETSI EN 300 417-9-1. The RFC says their work ensured global standards alignment.

With that standard complete, the RFC's intent is to document its use for PPP transport over SONET/SDH. The RFC itself defines no new framing or encoding for virtual concatenation.
sections.plainLanguage: The telephone-standards groups had already agreed how to tie channels together. This document just says how PPP should use that agreement.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security discussion in RFC 2615 also applies to this document. The RFC states that no new security features have been explicitly introduced or removed compared to RFC 2615.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing about safety changes. The same rules as before still apply.
